team-jardin.title: Team Jardin
team-jardin.context: SAE S3.01 - B.U.T. Computer Science, Year 2
team-jardin.description: A web application for a landscaping business: scheduling, invoicing and an employee portal.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: Our team of four - Sébastien Tremillon, Armin Osmanovic, Romain Duval-Cifoux and myself - designed and built this application during SAE S3.01 to address the daily needs of a small landscaping business.

The application combines a lightweight ERP and invoicing software, with the simplicity of tools such as Facture.net and the operational scheduling features of an ERP. Its centralised interface was designed for a business of 5 to 10 people.

features.title: Manager
features.description: Manages schedules, quotes and invoices, approves leave and oversees the business.

features.title: Employee
features.description: Views their schedule and job details, and submits leave requests.

features.title: Customer
features.description: Views invoices and job progress through a secure personal portal.

features.title: Business website
features.description: Project showcase, customer reviews and a contact form.

features.title: Scheduling
features.description: Daily, weekly and monthly views, staff assignments and automatic availability checks.

features.title: Invoicing
features.description: Custom quotes and invoices, PDF generation, payment tracking and automatic reminders.

features.title: Employee portal
features.description: Personal schedules, upcoming jobs and online leave requests.

features.title: Customer portal
features.description: Invoice and job tracking, profile updates and notifications before visits.

sections.title: Design process
paragraphs: We compared ERP tools (Axonaut, Odoo), invoicing software (Facture.net, Qonto) and scheduling tools (Calendly, Trello). We prioritised needs with MoSCoW, created Figma mockups and UML diagrams, and planned the work using WBS and Gantt charts.
This was our first project with a structured application architecture. We used MVC to separate views, data and business logic.

evidence.description: I worked across the development cycle: requirements, Figma mockups, PHP/MySQL development and deployment on DigitalOcean. My work included PDF invoice generation and the scheduling interface with three time views.
learnings: Apply good design and programming practices

evidence.description: We designed the conceptual data model from requirements and implemented MySQL with referential integrity. Scheduling queries were optimised to check employee availability.
learnings: Update and query a relational database

evidence.description: We used MoSCoW, WBS, Gantt charts and UML to prioritise, plan and document the project and meet deadlines.
The four-person team shared responsibilities, using GitHub for version control, Discord for daily communication and Google Docs for the design report.

movietor.title: MovieTor
movietor.context: Mobile development coursework - B.U.T. Computer Science
movietor.description: An Android app to discover films, series, actors and their connections, with a watchlist and favourites.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: Leny Arizzi, Aurélien Claudin and I took a mobile development assignment beyond its initial scope, building an Android application around a film and series database.
An external film API supplies titles, actors, ratings, trailers and cast information. Firebase handles authentication and persistent personal lists.

features.title: Watchlist
features.description: Save films and series to watch later.

features.title: Favourites
features.description: Mark favourite titles for quick access.

features.title: Video clips
features.description: Watch trailers and clips from a title's detail page.

features.title: Actor profiles
features.description: Explore actor information and connections to films and series.

features.title: Ratings and reviews
features.description: View ratings to help choose what to watch.

features.title: Search
features.description: Search the available film and series catalogue.

sections.title: Team
paragraphs: Leny Arizzi, Aurélien Claudin and I split the work by module: catalogue, detail screens and personal lists. Each of us contributed to the app's screens and features.

evidence.description: I developed Android screens in Kotlin and integrated the external API. I worked particularly on connections between actors and titles, and embedded video clips.
learnings: Apply good design and programming practices

evidence.description: I integrated Firebase Authentication so users could maintain their own persistent watchlist and favourites.
We coordinated the work across three developers to keep independently built screens consistent.

lumiere-mobilites.title: Lumière Mobilités
lumiere-mobilites.context: Development project - B.U.T. Computer Science, Semester 2
lumiere-mobilites.description: A Java/Swing application comparing route optimisation algorithms for Lyon's Festival of Lights.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: Antoine Panouillot, Nicolas Manesse and I built a tool to optimise routes between Festival of Lights locations using travelling salesman problem (TSP) algorithms.
The application supports Euclidean points on a custom coordinate plot and geographical points on an interactive map using JXMapViewer and OpenStreetMap tiles.

features.title: Two visualisations
features.description: Switch between a Euclidean plot and a geographical map according to the loaded data.

features.title: File import
features.description: Import point sets from text files, with automatic type detection.

features.title: Random generation
features.description: Generate Euclidean point sets to test the algorithms.

features.title: Four algorithms
features.description: Greedy, random, insertion and a custom greedy algorithm with 2-Opt optimisation.

features.title: Interactive editing
features.description: Add or remove points on the map with clicks and a context menu.

features.title: Route comparison
features.description: Save algorithm results and compare total distances.

sections.title: Algorithms
paragraphs: The greedy algorithm repeatedly chooses the nearest unvisited point. Random ordering provides a baseline. Insertion adds each point where it increases route length the least. Our custom approach starts with a greedy route and applies 2-Opt improvements to remove crossings and reduce total distance.

sections.title: Team
paragraphs: Antoine Panouillot, Nicolas Manesse and I shared the algorithm, data model and graphical interface work.

evidence.description: I developed a Swing interface with GridBagLayout, interchangeable views using CardLayout and JXMapViewer integration with pan, zoom and point selection.
learnings: Apply good design and programming practices
Integrate solutions into a production environment

evidence.description: I implemented and compared greedy, insertion and random algorithms, plus a custom approach with 2-Opt. The comparison feature makes the differences in route length visible.
Our three-person team coordinated the algorithm layer, Euclidean/geographical data model and user interface.

ultimatecourse.title: UltimateCourse
ultimatecourse.context: Graded Symfony assignment - B.U.T. Computer Science, Year 2
ultimatecourse.description: A Symfony shopping-list application with a multilingual catalogue, spending statistics and administration tools.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: Aurélien Claudin, Leny Arizzi and I built a V0 shopping-list application for a fictional entrepreneur as a proof of concept intended for investors. This second-year assignment explored Symfony beyond basic CRUD.
The technical requirements included Voter permissions, signup email verification, multilingual business data and custom validation constraints.

features.title: Secure authentication
features.description: Registration and login with email verification.

features.title: Shopping lists
features.description: Create, view and delete shopping lists, add products and manage quantities.

features.title: Spending statistics
features.description: Track total spending, average item cost, the most and least expensive items, and category breakdowns.

features.title: Multilingual interface
features.description: French, English and Japanese, with automatic price conversion to the local currency.

features.title: Administration
features.description: Full CRUD for products, product types and shops.

features.title: Custom validation
features.description: Validate entries, including a forbidden-word constraint.

sections.title: Technical choices
paragraphs: Gedmo Translatable stores translations of products, types and shops alongside Doctrine entities. SymfonyCasts Verify Email handles signup verification, with confirmation messages sent through Gmail. Faker PHP generates realistic test fixtures. Symfony Voters manage permissions between regular users and administrators, rather than relying on simple role checks in controllers.

sections.title: Team
paragraphs: Aurélien Claudin, Leny Arizzi and I shared entity and database management, business features and internationalisation. We coordinated delivery within the assignment deadline and prepared an oral presentation.

evidence.description: I built Symfony features including authentication, forms, Voter access rules and internationalisation. I wrote a custom forbidden-word Validator and configured an email verification bundle with Gmail delivery.
learnings: Apply good design and programming practices

evidence.description: I modelled Doctrine entities and relationships, created migrations and test fixtures, and wrote aggregate queries for totals, averages and category breakdowns.
learnings: Update and query a relational database

evidence.description: Our three-person team divided modules and coordinated delivery within the assignment's time limit, including an oral presentation.

stage-nperf.title: nPerf hosting request form redesign
stage-nperf.description: A React/TypeScript server-hosting request form, with PHP validation and automatic osTicket integration.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: nPerf measures internet connection performance using a worldwide network of over 3,000 partner-hosted test servers. Its previous hosting request form did not collect enough technical information.
Missing details led to repeated exchanges between support and customers, slowing network setup and server deployment. Without clear confirmation, some applicants submitted many duplicate tickets.

sections.title: My role
paragraphs: The project was part of a wider effort to improve server support efficiency. A guided, multi-step flow was intended to collect complete information at the first contact and reduce abandonment.

I worked independently on the form within an eight-person web team, covering the user journey, React frontend, translations, dark mode and a PHP backend that validates data and sends requests to osTicket.

features.title: Multi-step flow
features.description: Four request types: creation, modification, problem report and other, with tailored steps.

features.title: Two validation layers
features.description: React Hook Form validation for usability, backed by PHP server-side checks for data integrity.

features.title: Multilingual interface
features.description: French, English and Arabic, including right-to-left layout for Arabic.

features.title: Dark mode
features.description: Tailwind variables simplify theme maintenance.

features.title: osTicket integration
features.description: Automatic ticket creation with base64-encoded attachments.

features.title: Redux state management
features.description: A shared store makes form data available across components without prop drilling.

sections.title: First version and refactoring
paragraphs: The first version covered the use cases quickly but passed data through many components, sometimes with fourteen props. My supervisor's code reviews highlighted duplicated UI, unclear names, responsibility boundaries and accessibility issues.

I extracted shared components, centralised step routing through a mapping, moved state to Redux and reworked validation with React Hook Form. This reduced duplication and made the form easier for the team to maintain.

sections.title: Working methods
paragraphs: The web team used daily meetings, YouTrack tasks estimated in story points and code reviews before integration. Although I developed the form alone, regular team feedback helped me learn React, Redux and React Hook Form in a professional environment.

evidence.description: I built a React/TypeScript interface from the project specification, applying code review feedback to merge similar components, extract reusable elements and improve accessibility.
learnings: Write and implement functional and non-functional specifications from requirements
Apply good design and programming practices

evidence.description: I added server-side validation independently of client checks: rejecting malformed or private IP addresses, and checking attachment formats and sizes.
learnings: Understand how to secure data and code

evidence.description: I built the PHP integration with the osTicket API, including request-specific messages and base64 attachment encoding.
I tracked the work in YouTrack, breaking the project epic into tasks estimated in story points and translating requirements into features.
I joined an eight-person team, attended daily meetings and used code review feedback to improve both my code and how I asked for help.
learnings: Use interpersonal skills within a development team

annuaire.title: Annuaire
annuaire.context: Development project - B.U.T. Computer Science, Year 1
annuaire.description: A C customer directory with a paginated console interface, CSV files, sorting and filtering.

sections.title: Context
paragraphs: Ugo Lajoie and I built a customer directory in C for our first-semester development module. It needed to manage, display, sort, search and filter data while justifying the algorithmic choices.

sections.title: Data structures
paragraphs: Customer records are stored in an array of structures. A separate index array controls display, sorting and filtering, preserving the original data and making it possible to reset the view.

sections.title: Modularity
paragraphs: Dedicated functions build the menus, while shared functions such as user action prompts are reused across screens.

sections.title: Algorithm choices
paragraphs: Quick Sort orders the directory in average O(n log n) time. Linear search and cumulative filters run in O(n), supporting multiple combined selection criteria.

features.title: CSV import
features.description: Load customer data from a CSV file at startup.

features.title: Customer management
features.description: Add or remove customers and update the view.

features.title: Sorting
features.description: Sort by different criteria using Quick Sort.

features.title: Combined filters
features.description: Apply several filters together.

features.title: Console pagination
features.description: Browse the directory page by page in a text interface.

features.title: Modular menus
features.description: Navigate menus built from dedicated reusable functions.

evidence.description: I developed the directory in C, from CSV loading to adding, deleting and displaying customers in the console.
learnings: Apply good design and programming practices

evidence.description: I designed sorting and filtering operations to limit processing complexity: average O(n log n) Quick Sort and O(n) searches and filters.
I organised in-memory data using customer structures and a separate index array, with CSV files for persistence.
I analysed sorting, searching and filtering requirements and explained the algorithms chosen to meet them.
We worked as a pair on a modular design, separating functions and sharing development tasks.
